newsitem.title: UK: LIFFE March cocoa faces test of 865 after slide.
newsitem.headline: LIFFE March cocoa faces test of 865 after slide.

text.p: London cocoa futures faced a menacing test of 865 basis March on Tuesday as origins dumped more hedges in market persistently devoid of buyers, traders said.

A breach of the 865 low could trigger sell stops and drag the March contract to a fresh 18-month low of 847 stg in search for chart support on second month continuation basis, technical analysts said.
"Volumes are rather poor implying that there is an urgency in the selling," said one trader.

At midsession, March cocoa had shed 10 stg to stand at 870 stg a tonne but was above an intraday low of 868. Other contracts lost between five and 12 stg with total turnover reaching a modest 2,636 lots.
Traders noted some scale-down industry buying but this was largely outpaced by aggressive trade offers which chased overnight losses recorded in New York.
New York's March contract set a new 10-month low of $1,329 on Monday dragged by chart-driven speculative and origin selling.
London's turnover included a decent volume of switches as the March structure weakened slightly against the May to 21-22 stg. Traders also cited some AA deals on March.

Cocoa players were pinning hopes on the next set of arrival figures from West Africa to provide some sort of chart itinerary and pull the market from its range but the situation was confusing even there.

"Normally Ghanaian figures are the accurate barometer for the market but after the recent January jump in the Ivory Coast and the tardiness of recent data by the time they are of use they will be out of date," commented brokers GNI in a daily report.
Tuesday's news centred around the annual results of Nestle which announced a glowing 7.1 percent rise in 1996 total sales due to favourable exchange rates.
The company gave an upbeat assessment for 1997 saying sales would keep growing but there was no profit figure for 1996.

Sterling continued a moderately weak tone against the dollar trading at $1.6640, slightly above Monday's close. A CBI (Confederation of British Industry) report said sterling's strength was beginning to bite on exports but the case for a rate rise was finely balanced.
